items.label: f11-missing-key-401
items.front: ADR 0001: where does a Harbor API key travel, what happens when it is missing or unknown, and when can a response contain it?
items.back: Callers send a per-teammate key in the X-Api-Key header; a missing or unknown key is a 401. The key is returned exactly once, at creation, and no later response echoes it: TeammateResponse has no key field.

items.label: f08-measure-before-indexing
items.front: Harbor data guide: what does a controlled measure-before-indexing experiment record, and what must it show?
items.back: Synthetic data with several tenants and realistic variation in states and timestamps; record row counts, filters, generated SQL, warm-up strategy, repeated timings and result size; compare a candidate index with SQLite's query plan, then measure again. Count queries and substring searches can stay expensive even when few rows come back. Exit: one measured improvement, one preserved behavior, one limitation of the experiment.

items.label: f01-no-scheduler
items.front: Who drains Harbor's webhook outbox and wakes snoozed conversations, and how much does one dispatch call do?
items.back: Nobody automatically: there are only manual endpoints (wake-due, dispatch); the hosted services handle publication and exports. DispatchAsync claims one ready delivery at a time under a lease, at most 50 per call, serially, with limited retries - so eventual delivery is not promised.

items.label: f07-signature-header
items.front: ADR 0004: what does Harbor's webhook signature header look like, how is it compared, and when can you see the secret?
items.back: X-Harbor-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256>, a Stripe-style format. Compare signatures in constant time; WebhookSigner.TryVerify is the one definition shared by Harbor's tests and a real receiver. The signing secret is returned only once, at subscription creation, and never appears in a later response.

items.label: f05-paging-surface
items.front: ADR 0007: where do the page request and the paging metadata live in Harbor's list API, and why not an envelope?
items.back: The request uses query parameters ?page= (1-based) and ?pageSize=; the response carries X-Total-Count, X-Page, X-Page-Size and X-Total-Pages headers; bodies stay plain JSON arrays. A { data, total, page } envelope would have broken every existing client and test that expected plain arrays.

items.label: f06-attribute-string-map
items.front: ADR 0005: how are contact custom attributes stored and read in segment rules?
items.back: As a flat string map, so a comparison behaves the same whether the value arrived as "5" or 5. Rules address them as attributes.<key>, and SQL reads them with SQLite's json_extract, exposed to EF as a [DbFunction] on HarborDbContext; built-in fields map to columns.

items.label: f10-conversation-queries
items.front: ADR 0010: what is ConversationQueries, and what is it deliberately not?
items.back: A concrete component in the API project that consumes the API filter contract, accepts one evaluation time and a cancellation token, resolves segments within the workspace, and returns a no-tracking IQueryable; segment rule and query helpers moved to Infrastructure. It depends on EF and API contracts and is intentionally not a provider-independent repository abstraction.

items.label: f04-two-writer-conflict
items.front: Walk two writers through Harbor's optimistic concurrency: both load V1, A saves first. What happens to B, and what does the API return?
items.back: A's save changes the version; B's update still uses V1 as the original token, matches no row, and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, which the API maps to 409.

items.label: f09-list-vs-overview-shape
items.front: ADR 0010: once membership is shared, what does the list do with it, and what does the overview do?
items.back: The list applies a named ordering with an ID tie-breaker and then pagination. The overview performs one SQL aggregate over all matches and returns zeros for an empty population.

items.label: f02-evidence-statement
items.front: What is the testing workshop's evidence-statement template?
items.back: Given [fixture], when [operation], assert [observable result]. This catches [defect]. It does not prove [limit].

items.label: f03-fixture-row-purpose
items.front: In the queue filter test, why add an unrelated conversation that contains no search term?
items.back: Without it, a broken 'return everything' implementation could pass. Each fixture row should have a clearly different job: name the incorrect implementation it catches.

items.prompt: A test asserts that the list endpoint and the overview endpoint agree for several filters. Why is that not enough?

choices.text: Parity tests are flaky, because the two endpoints read in different transactions
The overview rounds its counts, so exact parity with the list can never be asserted at all
List paging means the two endpoints can never agree on totals in the first place
If both forget the workspace predicate they agree while leaking another tenant's data

choices: Parity tests are flaky, because the two endpoints read in different transactions
The overview rounds its counts, so exact parity with the list can never be asserted at all
List paging means the two endpoints can never agree on totals in the first place
If both forget the workspace predicate they agree while leaking another tenant's data

items.explanation: Parity proves consistency, not correctness. Check totals too: aggregates can leak without returning the foreign row.

items.prompt: Harbor appends Id ascending to every supported conversation ordering. What does that fix, and what does it not?

choices.text: It makes ordering total so static data pages reproducibly; a changing queue can still repeat or skip rows
It freezes the queue, so later pages can never repeat or skip a row even while writers insert
It turns offset paging into keyset paging, because Id is now the cursor
It only speeds the query up by letting SQLite walk the primary key index

choices: It makes ordering total so static data pages reproducibly; a changing queue can still repeat or skip rows
It freezes the queue, so later pages can never repeat or skip a row even while writers insert
It turns offset paging into keyset paging, because Id is now the cursor
It only speeds the query up by letting SQLite walk the primary key index

items.explanation: Rows can tie on timestamps; a unique order is required for pagination. Inserts or removals before the current offset still shift pages - a cursor or snapshot addresses that.

items.prompt: A conversation list is filtered with `?segmentId=`, so only conversations whose contact is in the segment should remain. How does ADR 0005 compose that filter?

choices.text: By reading a membership table that is refreshed when contacts change
By filtering the workspace's contacts in memory with a compiled rule
As a subquery over contact ids, so it stays a single SQL statement
By loading the matching contact ids first and passing them back in

choices: By reading a membership table that is refreshed when contacts change
By filtering the workspace's contacts in memory with a compiled rule
As a subquery over contact ids, so it stays a single SQL statement
By loading the matching contact ids first and passing them back in

items.explanation: ADR 0005 lines 23-29: SegmentCompiler.Compile builds an expression EF translates to a WHERE clause, and the conversation filter composes the segment as a subquery over contact ids (SegmentQueries.ContactIdsQuery), not a materialized list, so it stays one statement however many contacts match. Loading ids or filtering contacts in memory is the shortcut the Context rejects (lines 14-17), and membership is live, with nothing to refresh (lines 9-10).

items.prompt: A client calls a Harbor list endpoint with no paging parameters, then calls it again with ?pageSize=500. What does ADR 0007 say each call gets?

choices.text: The first page of 50, then a 400 for the pageSize over the limit
Every matching row, then a page of 500 as the max is advisory
The first page of 50, then a page whose size is capped at 200
Every matching row, then a 400 for the pageSize over the limit

choices: The first page of 50, then a 400 for the pageSize over the limit
Every matching row, then a page of 500 as the max is advisory
The first page of 50, then a page whose size is capped at 200
Every matching row, then a 400 for the pageSize over the limit

items.explanation: ADR 0007 lines 19-26: pageSize defaults to Paging.DefaultPageSize = 50 with a max of 200; omitting the parameters selects the first page, not everything, so the bound holds even for a caller that says nothing; out-of-range input is clamped, not rejected, so a pageSize over the max is capped. Only truly unparseable values such as ?page=abc still 400, via model binding (lines 39-41).

items.prompt: Harbor serializes a webhook payload once at publish time with pinned options and sends those bytes verbatim. What reason does ADR 0004 give?

choices.text: The dispatcher can no longer load the entities after the save commits
Receivers require camelCase names, which only publish-time options set
Re-serializing when sending could alter the bytes and void the signature
Storing the JSON once is cheaper than rebuilding it again for every retry

choices: The dispatcher can no longer load the entities after the save commits
Receivers require camelCase names, which only publish-time options set
Re-serializing when sending could alter the bytes and void the signature
Storing the JSON once is cheaper than rebuilding it again for every retry

items.explanation: ADR 0004 lines 34-39: the signed bytes must be reproducible independently of how the API renders responses, so the payload is serialized once at publish time with pinned options (Webhooks.PayloadJson) and sent verbatim; re-serializing at send time would change bytes and invalidate the signature, the same reason the outbox stores the exact payload. Cost, entity access and receiver casing are not the reasons the ADR gives.

choices.text: Wait for the key's built-in expiry to retire it within a day
Call the rotation endpoint, which keeps a short grace period
Revoke its bearer token at the OAuth server that issued it
Delete or re-issue that teammate's credential by hand

Lines 39-40: bearer-token/OAuth flows were rejected, so there is no token server to revoke at.

choices.text: It clashed with PageRequest.Page and silently ignored ?page=
It shadowed a route value, so asking for page 2 gave a 404
It clashed with the X-Page header, so the header was dropped
It failed to bind at all, so every list call returned a 400

items.explanation: ADR 0007 lines 34-38: a `[FromQuery] PageRequest page` collided with the object's own Page property and silently ignored ?page=, and every test passed because they all asserted page one. The rename to `paging` fixed it, and PaginationBoundaryTests walks to a real second page on every list endpoint to guard the regression. Nothing returned a 400 or 404, and the headers were not involved.

items.prompt: Per ADR 0002, how does a newly added Harbor endpoint end up with the right 403-versus-404 behavior, and what pins the distinction?

choices.text: Route attributes infer it from the URL; the OpenAPI document pins it
Each controller checks the workspace by hand; code review pins it
A global filter and per-query scoping; WorkspaceScopeMatrixTests pin it
A middleware looks the workspace up per request; request logs pin it

choices: Route attributes infer it from the URL; the OpenAPI document pins it

A global filter and per-query scoping; WorkspaceScopeMatrixTests pin it
A middleware looks the workspace up per request; request logs pin it

items.explanation: ADR 0002 lines 36-40: the rule is enforced in one global filter for scoped routes and one scoping predicate per resource query, so new endpoints inherit it by construction, and because it can look inconsistent at a glance the distinction is pinned by WorkspaceScopeMatrixTests. No per-controller check is relied on, the scoped-route 403 involves no database lookup, and routing metadata is not the mechanism.

items.prompt: ADR 0009 says every new conversation-creation path must go through ConversationStarter.StartAsync. What enforces that rule?

The compiler, as Conversation exposes only an internal constructor

items.explanation: ADR 0009 lines 37-42: ChannelParityTests runs one scenario down both channels and asserts equivalent results (same SLA, assignee and events), so a divergent new path is caught. The rule is a convention, not something the compiler enforces: a future contributor could write a controller that news up a Conversation directly, and the parity tests and the ADR are the guard rails. No constructor restriction, analyzer or trigger is involved.

items.prompt: An attacker holds a captured Harbor webhook that is now older than the receiver's tolerance. Per ADR 0004, why can the attacker not simply attach a fresh timestamp and resend it?

choices.text: Receivers take the time from the HTTP Date header, not the signature
Receivers store every timestamp they have seen and refuse repeats
Each delivery is bound to Harbor's IP, which the attacker cannot use
The HMAC covers the timestamp too, and re-signing needs the secret

choices: Receivers take the time from the HTTP Date header, not the signature
Receivers store every timestamp they have seen and refuse repeats
Each delivery is bound to Harbor's IP, which the attacker cannot use
The HMAC covers the timestamp too, and re-signing needs the secret

items.explanation: ADR 0004 lines 15-16 and 22-24: Harbor signs the string {timestamp}.{body} with HMAC-SHA256, and the receiver recomputes the HMAC over {t}.{body} with the shared secret and also rejects a t outside its tolerance. Changing the timestamp changes the signed string, so lines 29-31 conclude the attacker cannot re-stamp the request without the secret. The ADR uses the signed t, keeps no record of seen timestamps, and relies on no IP binding.

items.prompt: A teammate in workspace A sends a PUT to /api/contacts/{id} for a contact that really exists in workspace B. What status does ADR 0002 prescribe?

choices.text: 403 for this write, though a read of the same id would have been 404
409, as the contact exists but is owned by a different workspace
403, as a write to another tenant's resource is refused, not hidden
404, as the workspace-scoped lookup finds no such contact for them

choices: 403 for this write, though a read of the same id would have been 404
409, as the contact exists but is owned by a different workspace
403, as a write to another tenant's resource is refused, not hidden
404, as the workspace-scoped lookup finds no such contact for them

items.explanation: ADR 0002 lines 27-30: every resource query is scoped to the caller's workspace (c.WorkspaceId == User.GetWorkspaceId()), so a row the caller may not see is simply not found, identical to an id that never existed. Line 41: writes to a foreign resource also 404 rather than 403, for the same reason. Answering 403 or 409 here would confirm that the id exists in some other workspace, which is the oracle the ADR avoids.

items.prompt: Two conversations arrive at the same instant and both advance Inbox.LastAssignedTeammateId. Why does ADR 0006 leave that pointer without a concurrency token?

choices.text: A token would deadlock the two saves, as both lock the same inbox row

SQLite serializes the two writes, so this pointer update is never lost

items.explanation: ADR 0006 lines 15-18: a token would make the second writer's SaveChanges fail with DbUpdateConcurrencyException and a 409, but that save is committing a customer's new conversation along with the pointer bump, so failing it rejects an incoming customer message. The pointer is an ordinary column whose concurrent update is allowed to be lost; the worst case is one repeated teammate, which self-corrects on the next assignment (lines 29-31).

The ADR gives no publicity, mail-relay or rate-limit argument; the mail relay is listed only as one of the services that call Harbor.

items.prompt: Conversation has a version token and conflicting tracked writes raise a 409. A human reads a page, a colleague edits it, then the first human submits an update. What happens?

choices.text: It fails with 409, because the browser sent the version it originally read
It normally succeeds and overwrites, because the new request loads the latest version
The second request blocks until the colleague's transaction has closed
EF merges both edits field by field, keeping each human's changes
